title: Direct object pronouns: el, la, els, les
summary: Pronouns that replace the person or thing the action is done to.
explanation:
To avoid repeating a noun, Catalan replaces it with a weak (clitic) pronoun. Unlike English, where the pronoun comes after the verb (I see it), the Catalan pronoun goes before a conjugated verb:

  • Veus el gos? Sí, el veig. (Yes, I can see it, literally “I it see”.)
  • Coneixes la Maria? Sí, la conec. (Yes, I know her.)
  • Compres els llibres? Sí, els compro. (Yes, I’m buying them.)
  • Llegeixes les cartes? Sí, les llegeixo. (Yes, I’m reading them.)

The full set: em (me), et (you), el / la (him / her / it), ens (us), us (you, plural), els / les (them). English it has no single equivalent: a thing is el or la according to the gender of the noun it replaces (el pa → el compro; la clau → la busco). And beware the false friend: Catalan us means “you (plural)”; English “us” is ens.

Before a vowel or h, the singular forms are shortened to m’, t’, l’: M’escoltes? L’he vist. The plural forms are never shortened: els escolto.

Several verbs that need a preposition in English take a plain direct object in Catalan: esperar (wait for), escoltar (listen to), mirar (look at), buscar (look for). So I’m waiting for her is simply L’espero.

For a whole idea, or for “it / that” not referring to a specific noun, use the neuter ho: No ho sé. (I don’t know.)

With an infinitive, the pronoun can go before the helping verb or be attached to the end of the infinitive with a hyphen: La vull veure = Vull veure-la (I want to see her). After the infinitive, el and els become -lo and -los: Vull comprar-lo.

examples.ca: On és la clau? No la trobo.
examples.en: Where’s the key? I can’t find it.
We’ll be waiting for you in the square.

exercises.instruction: Replace the direct object with a pronoun.
Rewrite the sentence with the pronoun attached to the infinitive.

title: Indirect object pronouns: li, els
summary: To whom? The pronouns li (to him / her) and els (to them).
explanation:
The indirect object answers the question to whom? In English it usually comes with to (I gave the book to Marta) or sits straight after the verb (I gave Marta the book). The Catalan pronouns:

  • em: (to) me, et: (to) you, li: (to) him / her, and also (to) you when you address someone as vostè,
  • ens: (to) us, us: (to) you (plural), els: (to) them.

Examples:

  • Dono el llibre a la Marta. → Li dono el llibre. (I give her the book.)
  • Escric als meus pares. → Els escric. (I write to them.)

Note that li is the same for masculine and feminine, while els is both a direct object (“them”) and an indirect one (“to them”). English uses him / her in both roles, but Catalan keeps them apart: la veig (I see her) but li parlo (I talk to her).

Don’t let English decide for you: some verbs that take a plain object in English take a in Catalan. Trucar a algú and telefonar a algú (to call / phone someone) give li truco, whereas ajudar algú (to help someone) gives l’ajudo.

The noun and the pronoun are often used together for emphasis, which English never does: Li dic a la Maria. (I’m telling Maria, literally “I tell her to Maria”.)

examples.en: I’ve sent him (or her) a message.
I explain the lesson to them.
We like it a lot (literally “it pleases us a lot”).

exercises.instruction: Replace the indirect object with a pronoun.
Direct or indirect? Fill in el, la (l’) or li.

title: The pronoun en
summary: “Some”, “of them”, “about it”: quantities, parts and phrases with de.
explanation:
English has nothing quite like en (if you know French, it works much like French en). It replaces:

  • a noun with no article, or with a number or quantity word, where English says some, any, of them or nothing at all: Tens pa? Sí, en tinc. (Have you got any bread? Yes, I have.) Quantes germanes tens? En tinc dues. (How many sisters have you got? Two.)
  • a complement introduced by de: Parles de la feina? Sí, en parlo. (Do you talk about work? Yes, I talk about it.) Vens de Girona? Sí, en vinc. (Are you coming from Girona? Yes, I am.)

Before a vowel or h it becomes n’: N’he comprat tres. After an infinitive it is -ne, or ’n if the infinitive ends in a vowel: Vull comprar-ne. Vull beure’n.

Important: when there is a number or quantity and the noun itself is left out, en is compulsory. English is happy with “I’ve got two”, but in Catalan plain Tinc dues is wrong: say En tinc dues.

examples.ca: Vols cafè? No, gràcies, ja n’he pres.
examples.en: Would you like some coffee? No, thanks, I’ve already had some.

examples.ca: Quants anys tens? En tinc trenta.
examples.en: How old are you? I’m thirty (literally “I have thirty of them”).
I don’t know anything about it.

exercises.instruction: Answer using en and the hint in brackets.

title: The pronoun hi
summary: “There”, and how hi turns up in hi ha.
explanation:
hi replaces a place (introduced by a, en, dins, sota…). It is roughly English there:

  • Vas a Girona? Sí, hi vaig demà. (Yes, I’m going [there] tomorrow.)
  • Has estat a Mallorca? No, no hi he estat mai. (No, I’ve never been [there].)

The big difference: English usually leaves there out, but Catalan needs the pronoun. Sí, vaig demà on its own sounds incomplete.

hi also replaces a complement with a or en after verbs such as pensar en (think about), creure en (believe in), jugar a (play):

  • Penses en el viatge? Sí, hi penso molt. (Yes, I think about it a lot.)

The English preposition is no guide here: think about it is hi penso (because the verb is pensar en), but talk about it is en parlo (because the verb is parlar de, Unit 17). Always check which preposition the Catalan verb takes.

hi never changes form: before a vowel it is still hi (hi anem), and after an infinitive it is -hi: Vull anar-hi.

The hi in hi ha (Unit 3) is the same pronoun, “frozen” into the expression: it no longer refers to a place, just as the there in English there is doesn’t.

examples.ca: Viu a Reus? Sí, hi viu des de fa anys.
examples.en: Does he live in Reus? Yes, he’s lived there for years.
I can’t make head or tail of it.

exercises.instruction: Replace the place or the complement with hi.
en or hi? Fill in the gap.

title: Reflexive verbs: rentar-se
summary: Verbs with the pronoun -se: em rento, et rentes…
explanation:
In the dictionary, reflexive (pronominal) verbs end in -se: rentar-se (to wash), llevar-se (to get up), dir-se (to be called), dutxar-se (to have a shower).

English rarely uses myself, yourself… with everyday actions (I get up, I have a shower, I get dressed), but Catalan needs the pronoun every time. Without it the meaning changes: Rento el cotxe is “I wash the car”, Em rento is “I have a wash”.

The pronoun changes with the person and goes before the conjugated verb:

  • em rento, et rentes, es renta,
  • ens rentem, us renteu, es renten.

Before a vowel or h: m’, t’, s’: m’aixeco, t’aixeques, s’aixeca, but ens aixequem, us aixequeu, s’aixequen.

The plural forms can also mean “each other”: Ens veiem demà (see you tomorrow, literally “we’ll see each other”). And with parts of the body or personal belongings Catalan uses the article, not a possessive: Em rento les mans (I wash my hands).

With an infinitive the pronoun is attached with a hyphen and still agrees with the person: Vull dutxar-me = Em vull dutxar. (I want to have a shower.)

examples.ca: Com et dius? Em dic Emma.
examples.en: What’s your name? My name’s Emma (literally “I call myself Emma”).

exercises.instruction: Put the verb in the correct form with the right pronoun.

title: agradar: m’agrada, m’agraden
summary: The verb agrees with what is liked, not with the person who likes it.
explanation:
In English the person who likes is the subject: I like coffee. Catalan agradar works the other way round, like English please or appeal to: the thing that is liked is the subject and the verb agrees with it, while the person is an indirect object pronoun (Unit 16):

  • M’agrada el cafè. (I like coffee, literally “coffee pleases me”.)
  • M’agraden els gats. (I like cats, literally “cats please me”.)
  • M’agrada llegir. (I like reading.)

So the verb is singular or plural according to the thing, never the person: Ens agrada el cafè (we like coffee), Li agraden els gats (she likes cats). Notice too that Catalan uses the article (el cafè, els gats) for things in general, where English has none. And m’agrades means “I like you”, often in the sense “I fancy you”.

Pronouns: m’, t’, li, ens, us, els: Li agrada, ens agrada, els agraden.

For emphasis or contrast, add a mi, a tu, a ell…: A mi m’agrada el futbol, i a tu? (I like football. What about you?)

Short answers: A mi també (me too / so do I), A mi tampoc (me neither / nor do I), A mi sí / A mi no (I do / I don’t).

Interessar, encantar and fer mal work the same way: Em fa mal el cap (I’ve got a headache, literally “my head hurts me”).

examples.en: I don’t like this weather at all.

exercises.instruction: agrada or agraden?
Reply with “me too” or “me neither”.

title: Imperfet: parlava, feia, era
summary: The imperfect: habits and background description in the past.
explanation:
The imperfet describes habits and background in the past: what used to happen or what was going on. English has no single equivalent: depending on the context it comes out as used to, would, was / were + -ing or the simple past:

  • Quan era petit, jugava al carrer. (When I was little, I used to play in the street.)
  • Feia sol i estàvem contents. (It was sunny and we were happy.)
  • Mentre jo cuinava, ell llegia el diari. (While I was cooking, he was reading the paper.)

Don’t let English would lead you to the conditional: Every summer we would go to the beach is a past habit, so it’s Cada estiu anàvem a la platja, not aniríem.

Forms:

  • -ar: parlava, parlaves, parlava, parlàvem, parlàveu, parlaven
  • -er/-re and -ir: perdia, perdies, perdia, perdíem, perdíeu, perdien (dormia, servia…; verbs with -eix- drop it: llegeixo → llegia)

Irregular: ser → era, eres, era, érem, éreu, eren; fer → feia; dir → deia; veure → veia; creure → creia; riure → reia; treure → treia; viure → vivia; escriure → escrivia.

examples.en: We used to live in London.

examples.ca: Cada estiu anàvem a la platja.
examples.en: Every summer we would go to the beach.
What were you doing when I called you?

exercises.instruction: Put the verb in the imperfet.

title: Perfet: he parlat
summary: The present perfect: the past linked to a time period that isn’t over yet.
explanation:
The perfet is built like the English present perfect: the present of haver + past participle (I have spoken → he parlat):

  • he parlat, has parlat, ha parlat, hem parlat, heu parlat, han parlat

It is used when the time period in which something happened is not over yet: avui, aquest matí, aquesta setmana, aquest any, and for experience (mai, alguna vegada, ja, encara no):

  • Avui he treballat molt. (I’ve worked a lot today.)
  • Has estat mai a Andorra? (Have you ever been to Andorra?)

The overlap with English is large but not complete. Catalan uses the perfet even for a finished event, as long as it happened in the current period, where English prefers the simple past: Aquest matí he anat al mercat (I went to the market this morning). And for something that started in the past and is still going on, English uses the present perfect but Catalan uses the present: Visc aquí des de fa dos anys (I’ve lived here for two years).

Words like ja, mai and encara no normally go before the whole verb, not between the two parts as in English: Ja he dinat (I’ve already had lunch).

Participles: -ar → -at (parlat), -er/-re → -ut (perdut), -ir → -it (dormit). The most common irregular ones: fet, dit, vist, escrit, obert, pres, après, estat, tingut, pogut, volgut, sabut, vingut, viscut, begut, conegut, nascut, mort.

examples.ca: Aquest matí he anat al mercat.
examples.en: I went to the market this morning.

examples.ca: Mai no he vist la neu.

exercises.instruction: Put the verb in the perfet.

title: he menjat or vaig menjar?
explanation:
English also has two past forms (I have eaten / I ate), but Catalan chooses between the perfet (he menjat) and the passat perifràstic (vaig menjar) by a different rule: what matters is the time period. If you could add today or this…, use the perfet; if you could add yesterday or last…, use the perifràstic:

  • the period is still going on (avui, aquesta setmana, aquest any) → perfet: Avui he menjat paella. (I had paella today.)
  • the period is over (ahir, la setmana passada, l’any passat, el 2020) → passat perifràstic: Ahir vaig menjar paella. (I had paella yesterday.)

Compare:

  • Aquest any he viatjat molt. L’any passat vaig viatjar poc. (I’ve travelled a lot this year. I didn’t travel much last year.)
  • Aquest matí m’he llevat d’hora. Ahir em vaig llevar tard. (I got up early this morning. I got up late yesterday.)

Don’t be fooled by the form: vaig menjar is built with anar (“to go”), but it is a past tense: “I ate”. It has nothing to do with English I’m going to eat.

When no time is mentioned and you are talking about experience, use the perfet: Has estat mai a París? (Have you ever been to Paris?) When you tell a story made of clear, completed events in the past, use the perifràstic.

examples.ca: Avui he parlat amb la Núria.
Dilluns vaig parlar amb la Núria.
examples.en: I spoke to Núria on Monday.

examples.ca: Aquest mes he llegit tres llibres.
examples.en: I’ve read three books this month.

exercises.instruction: Choose the perfet or the passat perifràstic.

items.q: Fa dos anys (conèixer) ___ el meu marit.

title: Futur: parlaré
summary: The future tense and its irregular stems.
explanation:
English builds the future with a helper (will, going to); Catalan uses a single word. The future is formed from the infinitive plus the endings -é, -às, -à, -em, -eu, -an:

  • parlar → parlaré, parlaràs, parlarà, parlarem, parlareu, parlaran
  • dormir → dormiré, dormiràs…
  • verbs ending in -re drop the final -e: perdre → perdré

Irregular stems (same endings):

  • fer → faré, dir → diré, anar → aniré, ser → seré, haver → hauré
  • tenir → tindré, venir → vindré, voler → voldré, poder → podré, saber → sabré, valer → valdré

Two traps for English speakers:

  • Don’t copy going to with anar: vaig parlar means “I spoke” (Unit 23), and vaig a parlar for the future is avoided in careful Catalan. Use the future or the present.
  • For the near future Catalans often just use the present, much as English does with I’m working tomorrow: Demà treballo.

examples.ca: L’any que ve estudiaré a Barcelona.
examples.en: I’ll be studying in Barcelona next year.
Will you come to the party?

exercises.instruction: Put the verb in the future tense.

title: Condicional: parlaria, voldria
summary: Polite requests, wishes and advice: the Catalan for “would”.
explanation:
The conditional corresponds to English would (and often could or should). It is formed from the same stem as the future, with the endings -ia, -ies, -ia, -íem, -íeu, -ien, again one word, no helper:

  • parlar → parlaria, parlaries, parlaria, parlaríem, parlaríeu, parlarien
  • irregular: faria, diria, aniria, seria, hauria, tindria, vindria, voldria, podria, sabria

Main uses:

  • politeness: Voldria un cafè. (I’d like a coffee.) Podries ajudar-me? (Could you help me?)
  • wishes: M’agradaria viatjar més. (I’d like to travel more.)
  • advice: Jo, en el teu lloc, hi aniria. (If I were you, I’d go.)
  • conditions (with si + imperfet de subjuntiu, B2): Si tingués temps, ho faria. (If I had time, I’d do it.)

Two traps: English would for past habits is the imperfet, not the conditional (As a child I would read a lot → De petit llegia molt, Unit 21). And the conditional never goes in the si clause itself, just as standard English says if I had time, not if I would have time: si tingués temps, never si tindria temps.

examples.en: I’d like to book a table.
It would be better to wait.

exercises.instruction: Make the request more polite (use the conditional).
Put the verb in the conditional.

items.q: Jo, en el teu lloc, (anar) ___ al metge.

title: The imperative: parla! no parlis!
explanation:
In English the imperative is just the bare verb, and the negative simply adds don’t: Speak! / Don’t speak! In Catalan the positive and negative forms are different, and both depend on who you are talking to.

Positive commands:

  • tu: same as the 3rd person singular of the present (parla!, menja!, perd!, dorm!, llegeix!)
  • vosaltres: same as the 2nd person plural of the present (parleu!, perdeu!, dormiu!)
  • polite vostè / vostès: subjunctive forms (parli!, parlin!)

Negative commands are always no + subjunctive: no parlis!, no parleu!, no mengis! There is no word for don’t: no plus a different verb form does the job.

Irregular (for tu): ser → sigues, anar → ves, fer → fes, dir → digues, venir → vine, tenir → tingues, estar → estigues, saber → sàpigues.

Weak pronouns follow a positive command, joined with a hyphen or an apostrophe, as in English tell me!: Digues-me!, Dona’m el llibre! But in a negative command they go before the verb: No em diguis res! (Don’t tell me anything!)

examples.ca: Obre la finestra, si us plau.
Seguiu recte i gireu a la dreta.
examples.en: Go straight on and turn right.

exercises.instruction: Give the command for tu.
Make the command negative.

title: a, en, de with place names
summary: Where, where to and where from.
explanation:
English distinguishes in, at and to; with the names of towns and countries and with familiar places Catalan uses a for all three, both for location and for direction:

  • Visc a Barcelona. (I live in Barcelona.)
  • Vaig a Barcelona. (I’m going to Barcelona.)
  • Soc a casa / a la feina / a l’escola. (I’m at home / at work / at school.)

So English in is not automatically en: I live in London is Visc a Londres, not en Londres (that’s Spanish).

en is used before the indefinite article, demonstratives and quantity words:

  • Viu en un poble petit. (He lives in a small village.)
  • En aquest carrer hi ha molts bars. (There are lots of bars in this street.)

de marks origin and movement “from”:

  • Soc d’Anglaterra. (I’m from England.) Vinc de la feina. (I’m coming from work.)

Remember the contractions: a + el = al, de + el = del (Unit 4). Catalan also keeps the article where English often drops it: a la feina (at work), de l’escola (from school).

examples.en: Shall we go to the cinema?

examples.ca: Viuen en un pis molt gran.
examples.en: They live in a very big flat.
I’m coming back from Girona tomorrow.

exercises.instruction: Fill in a, al, en or de / d’ (adding the article where needed).

title: per and per a
summary: Cause and means versus purpose and recipient.
explanation:
English for covers both: thanks for everything (a cause → per) and a present for you (a recipient → per a). Catalan splits them, and per also does the work of English by, through, because of and (in order) to.

per expresses:

  • cause: Gràcies per tot. (Thanks for everything.) No surto per la pluja. (I’m not going out because of the rain.)
  • means: Parlem per telèfon. (We talk on the phone.)
  • route, “through”: Passo per la plaça. (I go through the square.)
  • exchange, price: L’he comprat per deu euros. (I bought it for ten euros.)
  • purpose, with an infinitive: Estudio català per treballar a Barcelona. (I’m learning Catalan [in order] to work in Barcelona.)

per a + a noun or pronoun expresses the recipient or the intended use:

  • Aquest regal és per a tu. (This present is for you.)
  • Un llibre per a nens. (A book for children.)

The simple rule since the IEC’s 2016 grammar: before an infinitive you can always use per; before a noun meaning “for someone / something” use per a. A quick test: if English for could be replaced by because of, in exchange for or through, it’s per.

examples.en: Thank you very much for the invitation.

examples.ca: Hi ha una carta per a vostè.

exercises.instruction: Fill in per or per a.

items.q: Aquestes flors són ___ la teva mare.
